title: 3-Read Friday #78: AI Homework, Coaching Premortems, and Participation
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton's 3-Read Friday #78 pairs an urgent AI-and-homework problem with two craft-focused pieces on coaching and participation. Jo Castelino tackles the question Barton had himself raised weeks earlier - whether AI has made maths homework obsolete - by proposing concrete strategies (similar in-class questions, narrated thinking, and building a culture where homework is visibly connected to lesson content) that preserve homework's value even when AI makes copy-paste completion trivially easy. Sarah Cottinghatt introduces the 'premortem' coaching technique, in which a coachee imagines a future failure has already happened and works backward to identify and pre-empt the barriers that would cause it, countering the natural optimism bias that assumes good intentions from a coaching conversation will translate automatically into classroom practice. Bronwyn Ryrie Jones opens a three-part series arguing that patchy student participation isn't a minor classroom-management nuisance but the central mechanism through which learning, explicit teaching, and inclusive culture either succeed or fail. Barton's framing threads a shared concern about visibility and accountability through gnarly AI-era homework problems, coaching follow-through, and classroom participation.
points: Jo Castelino's central proposal for AI-era homework: ask students the same or a similar question in the next lesson (in a controlled, AI-free environment) as a quick, low-stakes signal of whether homework effort actually happened.

Castelino draws on Craig Barton's own suggested solution - pairing AI-completable homework with an in-class paper quiz on the same content the next lesson - while flagging that low quiz scores don't always mean low homework effort, given how memory performance can fluctuate day to day.

Sarah Cottinghatt's premortem technique: rather than simply asking 'what could go wrong?', an effective premortem asks the coachee to vividly imagine a specific future moment of failure (e.g., 'it's Wednesday morning and you didn't script it') so they can concretely identify and pre-empt real barriers.

Cottinghatt frames the premortem as a direct antidote to the 'optimism bias' - the natural assumption that a coachee's commitment at peak motivation during a coaching conversation will survive contact with the busyness of daily teaching life.

Bronwyn Ryrie Jones's opening argument in her participation trilogy: student participation isn't just good for learning, it is the mechanism that makes explicit teaching possible at all - without visible participation, teachers 'are flying blind' about what students actually understand.
quotes: A few weeks ago, I asked the question: Is Maths homework dead? Homework expert, Jo, delves deeper into the issue, suggesting practical ways we can make homework useful in the age of AI.
A premortem is where you imagine that failure has already happened, analyse why this could have happened, and then take steps to prevent it from happening.
